sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
To efficiently scavenge ambient vibration energy and wind energy at the same time, a low-frequency piezoelectric harvester was designed, fabricated and tested. A lumped-parameter model of the cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester with a proof mass was established and the closed-form expressions of voltage and power on a resistance load under base acceleration excitation were derived. After effects of the lengths of the proof mass and electrodes on output power were analyzed, a MEMS harvester was optimally designed. By using aluminum nitride as piezoelectric layer, a MEMS energy harvester was fabricated with bulk micromachining process. Experimental results show that the open-circuit frequency of the MEMS harvester is about $1 3 4 . 8 \mathrm { H z }$ and the matched resistance is about $4 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Under the harmonic acceleration excitation of $\pm 0 . 1 \textrm { g }$ , the maximum output power is about $1 . 8 5 \mu \mathrm { W } .$ , with the normalized power density of about $6 . 3 \ : \mathrm { m W } \ : \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 } \ : \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 }$ . The critical wind speed of the device is between 12.7 and $1 3 . 2 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ when the wind direction is from the proof mass to the fixed end of the cantilever. The maximum output power under $1 6 . 3 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ wind is about $2 . 2 7 \ : \mu \mathrm { W } .$ .

(Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Such advantages as long lives, maintenance-free and so on make energy harvesters, which convert ambient solar/light power, mechanical power or thermal gradients into electrical energy, ideal electrical sources for wireless sensor nodes. Mechanical energy harvesters firstly convert ambient mechanical energy (such as vibration energy, fluid kinetic energy, impact energy etc) into the elastic potential energy and kinetic energy of micro structures and then convert the potential energy or kinetic energy into electrical energy by piezoelectric [1–6], electromagnetic [7, 8] or electrostatic [9, 10] transduction mechanisms. Vibration and wind energy harvesting have received much attention due to the ubiquitous presence of these energies in the environment [1, 3–12]. In recent years, harvesters fabricated by micromachining technologies have attracted increasing attention for the additional advantages of small volume, low cost and ease of integration with micro sensors and circuits [3–6, 8–10]. In this paper, the micromachined harvester for vibration and wind energy scavenging is of interest.

A resonance-based vibration energy harvester (VEH) produces high output power only when its natural frequency matches that of ambient vibration [1, 3, 13]. Once the frequency of the base excitation deviates from the natural frequency of the harvester, output power will decrease significantly. Dominant vibration frequencies of many natural environments (such as civil infrastructures, human bodies, trees etc) and that of many ‘man-made’ environments (such as motors or other machinery) are below $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ [14, 15], but natural frequencies of most MEMS harvesters reported are much higher than $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { \ H z }$ , which cannot efficiently scavenge the low-frequency vibration energy in these environments. Therefore, it is of significance to develop

MEMS harvesters with natural frequencies lower than $2 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ [13, 16–18].

More and more effort has been devoted to the study of wind energy harvesters (WEHs) over the past few years [10, 11, 19–26]. Compared with WEHs with rotating components [19, 20], flow-induced vibration WEHs are more compatible with micromachining technologies and more applicable to be miniaturized [11, 12, 21–23]. A flow-induced vibration WEH produces high output power only when wind speed is larger than the critical speed [12, 22, 23]. Although a large number of small-scale WEHs have been reported, there are only a few micromachined WEHs that have been reported. A WEH composed of a MEMS piezoelectric harvesting element and a Helmholtz resonator with cavity length of $3 . 5 \mathrm { c m }$ and diameter of $6 . 2 \mathrm { c m }$ produced maximum output power of $4 2 . 2 \mu \mathrm { W }$ under wind speed of $2 0 \mathrm { ~ m ~ s ~ } ^ { - 1 }$ [24]. An impact-based WEH mainly composed of a MEMS piezoelectric harvesting element, a flexible metal sheet and a stop produced maximum output power of about $1 . 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ under wind speed of $1 5 . 9 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ [25]. A micromachined piezoelectric harvester without proof mass was directly used to scavenging wind energy, but the output power was merely $3 . 3 \mathrm { n W }$ under wind speed of $1 5 . 6 \mathrm { m s ^ { - 1 } }$ [26].

Although there is vibration energy and wind energy at the same time in many environments, few harvesters were reported which can simultaneously scavenge vibration and wind energy. The aim of this paper is to develop a MEMS harvester which can scavenge ambient vibration energy and wind energy at the same time. After a lumped-parameter model of the cantilevered piezoelectric harvester with a proof mass was established, a MEMS energy harvester with the piezoelectric layer of aluminum nitride (AlN) was designed and micromachined. Then, the vibration energy harvesting performance and wind energy harvesting performance of the MEMS device were experimentally analyzed.

sections.heading: 2.1. Equation of motion
sections.text:
Piezoelectric cantilevers with a proof mass have been widely used to harvest ambient vibration energy [1, 3–6, 16]. The function of the proof mass is to enlarge the stress increment in the piezoelectric layer caused by inertial force under the base excitation. To optimize the MEMS cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester with a large proof mass, a lumped-parameter model was established in the following.

A cantilevered piezoelectric VEH is schematically shown in figure 1 [27–33]. It is assumed that the geometrical and material parameters of the cantilever are identical along the neutral axis $x$ . The distance from any point in the cross section to the neutral surface is denoted by coordinate z. A proof mass with length $l _ { m }$ , thickness $h _ { m }$ and width $^ b$ is fixed on the free end of the cantilever with length $l _ { b }$ and width $b$ . The cross section of the cantilever is composed of a structural layer with thickness $h _ { s }$ and a piezoelectric layer with thickness $h _ { p }$ on the top surface of the structural layer. Two metal electrodes are on the top surface and the bottom surface of the piezoelectric layer with $l _ { 0 } \ \leqslant \ x \ \leqslant \ l _ { 0 } + l _ { e }$ , which means that only this part of the piezoelectric layer converts vibration energy of the cantilever into electrical energy. The base excitation in the $z \cdot$ - direction at time $t$ is $w _ { b } ( t )$ . The deflection of the cross section with coordinate $x$ is denoted by $w ( x , t )$ . The displacement and rotation angle of the proof mass with respect to the base are denoted by $w _ { m } ( t )$ and $\alpha ( t )$ , respectively. The mass of the cantilever is much smaller than that of the proof mass and is neglected in the derivation of the lumped-parameter model. Because the deformation of the proof mass is negligible compared with that of the cantilever, it is reasonable to simplify the proof mass as a rigid body.

![](images/0659ae834083336da99e683548fb770aaa09771e78f1f7ec6287b11b9d8519bd.jpg)  
Figure 1. Schematic of a cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester.

A constitutive equation of the piezoelectric material is given by [27]

$$
T _ { 1 } ^ { p } = \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } S _ { 1 } ^ { p } - \bar { e } _ { 3 1 } E _ { 3 } ,
$$

where $T _ { 1 } ^ { p } , \ S _ { 1 } ^ { p }$ and $E _ { 3 }$ are the axial stress, axial strain and the electric field in the $z$ -direction, $\bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E }$ and $\bar { e } _ { 3 1 }$ are elastic constant under constant electric field and piezoelectric coupling coefficient of the material. According to equation (1), the inverse piezoelectric effect causes a stress increment of $\Delta T _ { 1 } ~ = ~ - \bar { e } _ { 3 1 } E _ { 3 }$ in the piezoelectric layers. The additional internal bending moment caused by the output voltage $v ( t )$ of the harvester can be written as [27]

$$
M _ { p } ( x ) = - [ u ( x - l _ { 0 } ) - u ( x - l _ { 0 } - l _ { e } ) ] \vartheta \upsilon ,
$$

where $u ( x )$ is a unit step function and $\vartheta$ is defined below.

The distance between the neutral surface and the bottom surface of the structural layer is

$$
z _ { u } = \frac { E _ { s } h _ { s } ^ { 2 } + \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } h _ { p } ( 2 h _ { s } + h _ { p } ) } { 2 E _ { s } h _ { s } + 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } h _ { p } } ,
$$

where $E _ { s }$ is Young’s modulus of the structural layer. The equivalent area moment of inertia of the cantilever is

$$
\begin{array} { c } { \displaystyle { I = \frac { b _ { b } h _ { p } ^ { 3 } } { 1 2 } + b _ { b } h _ { p } \left( h _ { s } + \frac { h _ { p } } { 2 } - z _ { u } \right) ^ { 2 } + \frac { E _ { s } b _ { b } h _ { s } ^ { 3 } } { 1 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } } } } \\ { \displaystyle { + \frac { E _ { s } } { \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } } b _ { b } h _ { s } \left( \frac { h _ { s } } { 2 } - z _ { u } \right) ^ { 2 } } } \end{array}
$$

and the coefficient $\vartheta$ is given by

$$
\vartheta = - 0 . 5 \bar { e } _ { 3 1 } b _ { b } ( h _ { p } + 2 h _ { s } - 2 z _ { u } ) .
$$

Neglecting the damping force on the cantilever, the internal moment on the cross section with the coordinate of $x$ is

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle M _ { t } ( \boldsymbol { x } ) = - m \left( \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } \right) ( l _ { b } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } - x ) } } \\ { ~ - \left( c _ { a 2 } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t } + c _ { a 1 } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } \right) ( l _ { b } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } - x ) , } \\ { ~ - [ u ( \boldsymbol { x } - l _ { 0 } ) - u ( \boldsymbol { x } - l _ { 0 } - l _ { e } ) ] \vartheta \boldsymbol { v } , } \end{array}
$$

where $m = \rho _ { m } l _ { m } b _ { m } h _ { m }$ is the mass of the proof mass, $\rho _ { m }$ is the density of the proof mass and $c _ { a 1 }$ and $c _ { a 2 }$ are damping coefficients of the proof mass with respect to deflection and base motion, respectively.

Substituting equation (6) into the deflection equation $\mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w / \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } x = M _ { t } ( x ) / \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I$ , the rotation angle $\alpha$ and the deflection $w _ { 1 }$ at the free end of the cantilever can be obtained by integration along $x$ axis. As the proof mass is simplified as a rigid body, the displacement of the center of the proof mass with respect to the base can be expressed as $w _ { m } = w _ { 1 } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } \alpha$ , which is given by

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle w _ { m } = - \frac { l _ { b } \left( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } \right) } { 1 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } \left[ m \left( \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } \right) \right. } } \\ { { \displaystyle \left. + \left( c _ { a 2 } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t } + c _ { a 1 } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } \right) \right] - \frac { l _ { e } ( 2 l _ { b } + l _ { m } - 2 l _ { 0 } - l _ { e } ) } { 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } \vartheta \upsilon . } } \end{array}
$$

According to equation (7), we obtain the equation of motion of the proof mass, given by

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { c _ { a 1 } } { m } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } + \frac { 1 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } { m l _ { b } ( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } ) } w _ { m } } } \\ & { } & { = - \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } - \frac { c _ { a 2 } } { m } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t } - \frac { 6 l _ { e } ( 2 l _ { b } + l _ { m } - 2 l _ { 0 } - l _ { e } ) } { m l _ { b } ( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } ) } \vartheta \upsilon . } \end{array}
$$

Then, the second derivative of the deflection with respective to coordinate $x$ is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } w } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } = - \frac { M ( l _ { b } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } - x ) } { \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } \left( \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } \right) } \\ { - \frac { 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } M ( l _ { b } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } - x ) } { \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } - \frac { 1 } { \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } \vartheta \boldsymbol { v } . } \end{array}
$$

The average strain in the piezoelectric layers is given by [27]

$$
\bar { S } _ { 1 } ^ { p } = - h _ { p c } \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } w } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } ,
$$

where $h _ { p c }$ is the distance from the center of the piezoelectric layer to the neutral axis. The average electrical displacement in the piezoelectric layer is

$$
\bar { D } _ { 3 } = \bar { e } _ { 3 1 } S _ { 1 } ^ { p } + \bar { \varepsilon } _ { 3 3 } ^ { S } E _ { 3 } ,
$$

where $\bar { \varepsilon } _ { 3 3 } ^ { S }$ is the permittivity under constant stress and $E _ { 3 } =$ $- v ( t ) \big / \bar { h _ { p } }$ is the electric field intensity in the $z$ -direction.

The current through the resistor can be expressed as

$$
\int _ { A } \frac { \mathrm { d } \bar { D } _ { 3 } } { \mathrm { d } t } \mathrm { d } A = \frac { v ( t ) } { R _ { 1 } } .
$$

According to equations (13)–(16), we obtain the coupled electrical circuit equation

$$
C _ { p e } \frac { \mathrm { d } \upsilon ( t ) } { \mathrm { d } t } + \frac { 1 } { R _ { 1 } } \upsilon ( t ) = i _ { p } ( t ) ,
$$

sections.heading: 2.2. Closed-form expression of undamped natural frequency
sections.text:
Neglecting the damping force and base excitation, the equation of free vibration of the proof mass with electrical short-circuit (that is $v ( t ) = 0$ ) is simplified as

$$
\frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { 1 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } { m l _ { b } \left( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } \right) } w _ { m } = 0 .
$$

The undamped natural frequency of the harvester is given by

$$
f _ { n } = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \sqrt { \frac { 1 2 \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } { m l _ { b } \left( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } \right) } } .
$$

By neglecting the damping corresponding to base movement, equation (8) can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } + \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } } \\ & { } & { = - \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } - \frac { 6 l _ { e } ( l _ { b } + l _ { m } - l _ { 0 } ) } { M l _ { b } ( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } ) } \vartheta \boldsymbol { \nu } , } \end{array}
$$

where $\omega _ { n } ~ = ~ 2 \pi f _ { n }$ and mechanical damping ratio $\begin{array} { r l } { \xi _ { n } } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $c _ { a 1 } / 2 m \omega _ { n }$ .

sections.text:
In this section, the governing circuit equation was derived when the harvester is electrically connected with a resistor with the resistance of $R _ { 1 }$ . Neglecting the damping force corresponding to base movement, the total bending moment at $l _ { 0 } \leqslant x \leqslant l _ { 0 } + l _ { e }$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle M _ { t } ( x ) = - M ( l _ { b } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } - x ) \left( \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } \right) } } \\ { { \displaystyle ~ - 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } M ( l _ { b } + 0 . 5 l _ { m } - x ) \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } - \vartheta \boldsymbol { v } . } } \end{array}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { C _ { p e } \ = C _ { p } - \frac { \bar { e } _ { 3 1 } \vartheta h _ { p c } b _ { b } l _ { e } } { \bar { c } _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } I } , \quad C _ { p } = \frac { \bar { \varepsilon } _ { 3 3 } ^ { S } b _ { b } l _ { e t } } { h _ { p } } , } \\ & { i _ { p } ( t ) = \frac { K _ { m m } } { \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } } \left( \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 3 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 3 } } + 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { d ^ { 3 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 3 } } \right) , } \\ & { K _ { m m } = \frac { 6 \bar { e } _ { 3 1 } h _ { p c } b _ { b } l _ { e } ( 2 l _ { b } + l _ { m } - 2 l _ { 0 } - l _ { e } ) } { l _ { b } \left( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } \right) } , } \end{array}
$$

where $l _ { e t }$ is the equivalent length of the electrodes for the evaluation of the capacitance.

sections.text:
The closed-form expressions of the response under harmonic base acceleration of $\mathrm { d } w _ { b } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } = A _ { 0 } \mathrm { e } ^ { \mathrm { i } \omega t }$ can be obtained from the equation of motion of the proof mass and the coupled electrical circuit equation. It is assumed that the voltage on the resistor is $v ( t ) = V e ^ { \mathrm { i } \omega t }$ . Equation (11) can be expressed as

$$
\frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } \frac { \mathrm { d } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t } + \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } = - \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } - \chi _ { v } v ( t ) ,
$$

where

$$
\chi _ { v } = \frac { 6 l _ { e } ( 2 l _ { b } + l _ { m } - 2 l _ { 0 } - l _ { e } ) \vartheta } { M l _ { b } \left( 4 l _ { b } ^ { 2 } + 6 l _ { b } l _ { m } + 3 l _ { m } ^ { 2 } \right) } .
$$

Substituting $i _ { p } ( t )$ in equation (18) into equation (17), we obtain

$$
C _ { p e } \frac { \mathrm { d } v \left( t \right) } { \mathrm { d } t } + \frac { v \left( t \right) } { R _ { 1 } } = \frac { K _ { m m } } { \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } } \left( \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 3 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 3 } } + 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 2 } w _ { m } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 2 } } + \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ { 3 } w _ { b } } { \mathrm { d } t ^ { 3 } } \right) .
$$

It is assumed that the displacement of the proof mass with respect to the base is given by $w _ { m } ( t ) = H _ { W } ( \omega ) A _ { 0 } \mathrm { e } ^ { \mathrm { i } \omega t }$ and the

output voltage is given by $v ( t ) = H _ { V } ( \omega ) A _ { 0 } \mathrm { e } ^ { \mathrm { i } \omega t }$ . According to equations (19) and (21), we obtain

$$
H _ { W } ( \omega ) = - \frac { c _ { n } ( \omega ) } { a _ { n } ( \omega ) c _ { n } ( \omega ) - \chi _ { v } } ,
$$

and

$$
H _ { V } ( \omega ) = \frac { 1 } { a _ { n } ( \omega ) c _ { n } ( \omega ) - \chi _ { v } } ,
$$

where

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle c _ { n } ( \omega ) = \frac { C _ { p e } } { K _ { m m } } + \frac { \chi _ { v } } { \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } } + \frac { 1 } { \mathrm { i } R _ { 1 } K _ { m m } \omega } , } \\ { \displaystyle a _ { n } ( \omega ) = - \omega ^ { 2 } + \mathrm { i } 2 \xi _ { n } \omega _ { n } \omega + \omega _ { n } ^ { 2 } . } \end{array}
$$

The amplitude of voltage on the resistor can be expressed as

$$
V = H _ { V } ( \omega ) A _ { 0 } ,
$$

and output power is

$$
P = \frac { H _ { V } ^ { 2 } ( \omega ) A _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } } { 2 R _ { 1 } } .
$$

sections.heading: 3.1. Optimization
sections.text:
In this section, a MEMS piezoelectric energy harvester was optimally designed according to the lumped-parameter model. The target for the optimization is to scavenge maximum power with the same chip area. For a high electromechanical coupling coefficient, good compatibility with silicon micromachining process and excellent chemical stability, AlN was used as the piezoelectric material. The thickness of the AlN was set as $1 . 3 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The thickness of the proof mass was set as $5 1 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , which is close to the thickness of the 4 inch (1 1 0) silicon wafer. Both the width of the cantilever and that of the proof mass were set as $8 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ . The silicon structural layer of the cantilever was set as $3 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The total length of the harvester $l _ { t }$ is the sum of the length of the cantilever $l _ { b }$ and that of the proof mass $l _ { m }$ , which means $l _ { t } = l _ { b } + l _ { m }$ . It is assumed that the length of the harvester is kept unchanged as $l _ { t } = 1 0 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The density and the Young’s modulus of the single-crystal silicon used in the optimization are $\rho _ { s } = 2 . 3 \times 1 0 ^ { 3 } \mathrm { k g } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 3 }$ and $E _ { s } = 1 6 9 \mathrm { G P a }$ [34]. The elastic constant, piezoelectric coupling coefficient and permittivity of AlN material are $c _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } = 3 3 1 ~ \mathrm { G P a }$ , $e _ { 3 1 } = - 0 . 5 8 \mathrm { ~ C ~ m } ^ { - 1 }$ and $\varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { s } = 8 . 9 \varepsilon _ { 0 }$ [35, 36], respectively. The mechanical damping ratio was set as $0 . 1 \%$ [3]. Such geometrical parameters as the length of the proof mass and the length of the electrodes need to be optimized. The base acceleration amplitude was set as $1 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 2 }$ in the optimization. To obtain high output power, the natural frequency of the harvester needs to match the frequency of the ambient vibration. The influence of the proof mass length on the natural frequency was analyzed first. When the proof mass length changes from 0.3 to 0.8 times the total length of the harvester, the calculated undamped natural frequency of the harvester from equation (10) is shown in figure 2. There is a minimum frequency when length of the proof mass changes. ![](images/e7ae501b11f8bcadc37066884214d248fb2d6a39b3b5e8b2035ce7fb2a9d90ba.jpg) Figure 2. Undamped natural frequency versus length ratio of proof mass to cantilever. ![](images/a7048ba9b56650ba9e379fc4d868ec5b2bd918bdd55236dfae1a2cea950d03eb.jpg) Figure 3. Normalized power versus length ratio of electrode to cantilever. With increasing proof mass length, both the mass of the proof mass and the stiffness of the cantilever increase. When the proof mass length is short (shorter than 0.4 times total length), the decrease of the mass is comparatively more obvious than the decrease of the stiffness with the decrease of the proof mass length, which makes the undamped natural frequency increase. When the proof mass length is long (longer than 0.6 times total length), the increase of stiffness is comparatively more obvious than that of the mass with the increase of the proof mass length, which also makes the undamped natural frequency increase. The effect of electrode length on maximum output power for load resistance between $1 0 \mathrm { ~ k } \Omega$ and $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ was analyzed. For several length ratios of proof mass to harvester, the simulated maximum output power from equation (26) versus the length ratio of the electrodes to cantilever is given in figure 3. The output power corresponding to a specified $l _ { m } / l _ { t }$ was normalized with respect to the maximum power with the same $l _ { m } / l _ { t }$ . When the length ratio $l _ { m } / l _ { t }$ equals 0.3 and 0.4, the length ratio $l _ { e } / l _ { b }$ corresponding to the maximum output power is about 0.82 and 0.89, respectively. When the length of the proof mass is longer than 0.5 times the total length of the harvester, which means $l _ { m } / l _ { t } \geqslant 0 . 5$ , the length of the electrodes corresponding to the maximum output power is about the length of the cantilever. In other words, to obtain high output power, the electrode length may be set as the cantilever length when the length of the proof mass is longer than 0.5 times the total length of the harvester. ![](images/78f8410550097b6b18afd9e9be6d81ab362ad7e988c89e5a982d17738ecfa65e.jpg) Figure 4. Maximum power versus length ratio of proof mass to harvester. The influence of the length of the proof mass on the maximum power was analyzed to obtain the optimized proof mass length. With the proof mass length between 0.3 and 0.8 total length, the electrode length between 0.5 and 1 times cantilever length and the load resistance between $1 0 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ , simulated normalized maximum power from equation (26) versus the length ratio of the proof mass to the harvester is shown in figure 4. There is a maximum output power when proof mass length changes. The output power reached the maximum value when the length ratio of the proof mass to harvester is about 0.72. Table 1. sections.heading: 3.2. Fabrication of MEMS piezoelectric energy harvester
sections.text:
MEMS piezoelectric harvesters were fabricated with the process flow shown in figure 5. A 4 inch (1 1 0) oriented ntype silicon wafer was used as the substrate. After a silicon oxide layer of thickness $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ was thermally oxidized at $1 0 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , a titanium/platinum layer of thickness $4 0 \mathrm { n m } / 1 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was deposited by sputtering and patterned by a lift-off process. Afterward, an AlN seed layer of thickness about $2 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ was reactively sputtered and a molybdenum layer of thickness about $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ was sputtered. After an AlN film of thickness about $1 . 3 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the preferential (0 0 2) orientation perpendicular to the substrate was reactively sputtered and patterned as the piezoelectric layer [37, 38], an Al layer of thickness about $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was sputtered and patterned as the top electrodes. Then, release slots with depths of about $3 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ on the front side of the substrate were etched by deep reactive ion etching (DRIE). After an Al layer of thickness about $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ was sputtered and patterned on the back side of the substrate as the mask, the MEMS energy harvesters were released by DRIE from the back side of the substrate. Photographs of a micromachined piezoelectric energy harvester are shown in figure 6. The thickness of the single-crystal silicon structural layer of the cantilever was about $3 0 \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ .

![](images/471fc7fd10ace505a83a0a9d390856f629ab61ea41fa003d9ee95f0a49ecbdd7.jpg)  
Figure 5. Process flow of MEMS piezoelectric energy harvester.

![](images/bf75d60bd884cf7f739b2ea4373700776b970cabcc29f216614020a0ce51e750.jpg)  
Figure 6. Photographs of a MEMS energy harvester.

sections.heading: 4.1. Performance of vibration energy harvesting
sections.text:
The vibration energy harvesting performance of the MEMS energy harvester was measured on an electromagnetic shaker. The harvester was mounted on the shaker by a fixture. A sinusoidal voltage signal from an oscillograph was enlarged by a power amplifier to drive the electromagnetic shaker. Acceleration of the shaker was monitored by an accelerometer. Output voltage of the harvester was monitored by oscillograph. All measurements were carried out under acceleration with constant amplitude of $0 . 1 g$ (where $g = 9 . 8 \mathrm { ~ m ~ s ^ { - 2 } }$ ).

The simulated and measured root-mean-square (RMS) open-circuit voltage of the harvester versus the frequency of the base excitation was given in figure 7. The open-circuit natural frequency (anti-resonance frequency) of the harvester is about $1 3 4 . 8 \mathrm { H z }$ with the maximum RMS open-circuit voltage of about 1.42 V. The half power bandwidth was about $0 . 2 3 7 \%$ and the quality factor was about 421, which was very close to that of the unpackaged harvester in [31]. The RMS voltages on resistors with different electrical resistances were recorded at the anti-resonance frequency. Figure 8 gives the measured RMS voltage and corresponding output power versus electrical resistance. The matched resistance is about $4 1 0 { \mathrm { ~ k } } \Omega$ at the open-circuit frequency and the maximum output power is about $1 . 8 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ under the base excitation of $\pm 0 . 1 \ g$ , with the normalized power density of about $6 . 3 \ : \mathrm { m W } \ : \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \ : g ^ { - 2 }$ .

![](images/b525444da4cad1384d668f97d962250b89eadcb0661559c850ffb9a236e66441.jpg)  
Figure 7. RMS open-circuit voltage versus frequency under $0 . 1 g$

![](images/60ae2a25ff3be958bd904e371cef370fb7145dd9c7ae8efbc6f5f84fb976c82b.jpg)  
Figure 8. Voltage and power versus electrical resistance at anti-resonance frequency.

sections.heading: 4.2. Performance of wind energy harvesting
sections.text:
The wind energy harvesting performance of the MEMS piezoelectric energy harvester was then measured in a small wind tunnel with the maximum wind speed of about $1 6 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The harvester was mounted onto a fixture at the center of the working section of the wind tunnel. The wind speed at the center of the working section was manually controlled by a variable frequency motor and was measured by an anemometer with the resolution of $0 . 1 \mathrm { ~ m ~ } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The time history of the voltage on the $4 1 0 { \mathrm { ~ k } } \Omega$ resistor is monitored and recorded by oscillograph. When wind speed was zero, the RMS voltage on the resistor was lower than $0 . 6 \mathrm { m V } ,$ , which means that the RMS voltage noise is below $0 . 6 \mathrm { m V } .$

When the wind direction was from the proof mass to the fixed end of the cantilever and wind speed increased from 0.6 to $1 6 . 3 \mathrm { ~ m ~ s ^ { - 1 } }$ , the measured RMS voltage on the $4 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistor in $2 0 ~ \mathrm { s }$ and corresponding output power are given in figure 9. When wind speed increased from 0.6 to $2 . 7 ~ \mathrm { m ~ s ^ { - 1 } }$ , noise dominated the output and the RMS voltage was almost unchanged as $0 . 6 \ \mathrm { m V } .$ The RMS voltage reached $1 . 3 2 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ when wind speed reached $3 . 1 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , where intermittent voltage waveforms appeared on the oscillograph. When wind speed increased from 3.1 to $1 2 . 7  { \mathrm { ~ m ~ s ~ } } ^ { - 1 }$ , RMS voltage increased slowly from 1.32 to $9 7 . 3 ~ \mathrm { \ m V } .$ The intermittent voltage waveforms are clearly demonstrated in the time history of the voltage under $7 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m ~ s ^ { - 1 } }$ wind in figure $1 0 ( a )$ . As shown in figure $1 0 ( b )$ , the frequency corresponding to the maximum FFT amplitude of the voltage was about $1 3 4 . 3 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , which is very close to the natural open-circuit frequency of the harvester. When the wind speed increased to $1 3 . 1  { \mathrm { ~ m ~ } }  { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ , the RMS voltage increased substantially to $7 4 4 \ \mathrm { \ m V } ,$ , and stable near resonant time history of voltage on the resistor was observed, as shown in figure $1 0 ( c )$ . The frequency corresponding to the maximum FFT amplitude of the voltage was about $1 3 0 . 8 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , as shown in figure $1 0 ( d )$ . The measured critical wind speed of the harvester is between 12.7 and $1 3 . 1  { \mathrm { ~ m ~ } }  { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ . The output power increased about 57 times from $2 3 \mathrm { \ n W }$ to $1 . 3 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ when wind speed increased from $1 2 . 7 \mathrm { ~ m ~ s ~ } ^ { - 1 }$ (which is a little lower than the critical speed) to $1 3 . 1 \ : \mathrm { ~ m ~ } \ : \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ (which is a little higher than the critical wind speed). When the wind speed increased from 13.1 to $1 6 . 3  { \mathrm { ~ m ~ } }  { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ , the voltage and output power increased and stable near resonant time histories of output voltage were also observed. The RMS voltage and output power were $9 6 5 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ and $2 . 2 7 \ \mu \mathrm { W } ,$ , respectively, when wind speed was $1 6 . 3 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ .

![](images/9ef100bfea06c9b92bd29982c21276843b085b54ebd1e31de2adeaf64f147d84.jpg)

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text:
Micromachined cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvesters can be used to scavenge ambient vibration energy and wind energy at the same time. A lumped-parameter model of the cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester with a proof mass was established and closed-form expressions of voltage and output power on resistance load were derived. To obtain high output power under the accelerometer excitation with constant amplitude, the length ratio of the proof mass to harvester and that of the electrode to cantilever should be optimized. For the given thicknesses of the structural layer, piezoelectric layer and proof mass, the output power reached a maximum value when length ratio of the proof mass to harvester is about 0.7 and the length of the electrodes may be set as the length of the cantilever when the proof mass is longer than the cantilever.

By using AlN with the thickness of about $1 . 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ as the piezoelectric layer, an MEMS energy harvester was micromachined by the bulk micromachining process. Experimental results show that the open-circuit frequency of the MEMS harvester is about $1 3 4 . 8 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and the matched resistance is about $4 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Under the harmonic acceleration excitation of $\pm 0 . 1 ~ g$ at the open-circuit frequency, the maximum output power is about $1 . 8 5 \mu \mathrm { W }$ with the normalized power density of about $6 . 3 \mathrm { \ m W \ c m ^ { - 3 } \ } g ^ { - 2 }$ . When the wind direction is from the proof mass to the fixed end of the cantilever, the critical wind speed of the harvester is between 12.7 and $1 3 . 2 \mathrm { ~ m ~ s ~ } ^ { - 1 }$ . The maximum output power under $1 6 . 3 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ wind is about $2 . 2 7 \ \mu \mathrm { W } .$ .
